description: Per-translation glossary overlay for the Wheel of Heaven Translation of Joshua (Former Prophets wave 1: chapters 5, 6, 10, the canon-cited chapters). v1.0.0 (2026-11-01, Editor pass, claude-opus-5-5) creates the overlay. It holds nine conventions shared verbatim by the joshua-woh, judges-woh and 1-samuel-woh overlays, each applying without change of substance the founder-ratified (2026-11-01) entry of the same name in the 1-kings-woh / 2-kings-woh overlays (suffix -kings): Hebrew proper-name transliteration, the elohim referent/article rule (extended by clauses 6 and 7 for an anarthrous narrative subject and an attributive adjective), the 'man of the Elohim' title, the nefesh scope, the ruach transliteration, Ketiv/Qere, the MT baseline, 'YHWH of hosts' and Ba'al. Shared entries carry identical text and appliesTo (refIds of all three books) in all three overlays; extend them together. The Kings shofar decision is proposed for central promotion (shofar-rams-horn-signal-instrument-cross-corpus, wave-FP1 central diff) and is not duplicated here; the Kings gahar and torah entries have no sites in this wave. Candidates for later promotion to central: the shared conventions as a Former Prophets set, and herem (joshua-woh). Book-specific decisions: śar-ṣəḇāʾ-YHWH 'the captain of the host of YHWH' (5:14-15); ḥērem 'devoted' / 'devote to destruction' (6:17-21; 10); the shout and the falling wall (6:5-20); 'great stones from the skies ... hailstones' (10:11); the sun and moon standing still (10:12-13); 'the Book of Yashar' (10:13). Signed off at human review on 2026-11-01 (zarazinsfuss); this wave's central proposals were applied as central glossary v2.86.0, and the sign-off merge is v2.90.0.

entries.lemma: Hebrew personal names, toponyms and gentilics of Joshua, Judges and 1 Samuel
entries.partOfSpeech: proper nouns and gentilic adjectives - book-wide rendering convention
entries.literal: the Hebrew name forms as written in the Masoretic Text
entries.standardEnglish: the conventional English (KJV/ASV) forms: Joshua, Jericho, Gideon, Samson, Samuel, Saul, Goliath, Philistine ...
entries.wohChoice: WoH transliteration of the Hebrew name, under the founder-ratified Kings convention (1-kings-woh / 2-kings-woh `hebrew-proper-name-transliteration-convention-kings`, ratified at human sign-off 2026-11-01): Hebrew long forms; tz for tsade; ʿayin and aleph marked with an apostrophe where the Kings table does; gentilics in -î take English '-ite' on the transliterated stem; a small set of names fixed in English usage is kept in English (here Gilgal, David, Asherah, the Levites); and each chapter title adds the English form of its principal name in parentheses. Equivalence table. Joshua 5, 6, 10: Yehoshua = Joshua; Nun = Nun; Yarden = Jordan; Yericho = Jericho; Mitzrayim = Egypt; Kena'an = Canaan; Yisra'el = Israel; Rachav = Rahab; Adoni-Tzedeq = Adoni-zedek; Yerushalayim = Jerusalem; Giv'on = Gibeon; Hevron = Hebron; Pir'am = Piram; Yarmut = Jarmuth; Yafia = Japhia; Lakhish = Lachish; Devir = Debir; Beit-Choron = Beth-horon; Azeqah = Azekah; Maqqedah = Makkedah; Ayyalon = Aijalon; Livnah = Libnah; Qadesh-Barnea = Kadesh-barnea; Azzah = Gaza; the Negev (hanneḡeḇ; ASV 'the South'); Ai, Hoham, Eglon, Horam, Gezer and Goshen are identical in both forms; gentilics 'the Emorites' (hāʾĕmōrî; ASV 'the Amorites') and 'the Kena'anites' (hakkənaʿănî; ASV 'the Canaanites'); the descriptive toponym gibʿaṯ hāʿărālôṯ is translated 'the hill of the foreskins' (ASV). Judges 6, 13: Midyan = Midian; Amaleq = Amalek; Ofrah = Ophrah; Yo'ash = Joash; Avi'ezer = Abiezer, 'the Avi'ezrite(s)' = the Abiezrite(s); Gid'on = Gideon; Menasheh = Manasseh; Zevulun = Zebulun; Naftali = Naphtali; Yizre'el = Jezreel; Yerubba'al = Jerubbaal; the altar name YHWH-Shalom = Jehovah-shalom (as genesis-woh 'YHWH-yir'eh', Gen 22:14); Tzor'ah = Zorah; 'the Danites'; Manoach = Manoah; Shimshon = Samson; Machaneh-Dan = Mahaneh-dan; Eshta'ol = Eshtaol; Asher identical; bənê-qeḏem translated 'the children of the east' (ASV). 1 Samuel 3, 5, 6, 17: Shemu'el = Samuel; Be'er Sheva = Beersheba (central be-er-sheva-folk-etymology); Even-Ha'ezer = Eben-ezer; 'the Ashdodites'; Gat = Gath; Eqron = Ekron, 'the Eqronites'; Par'oh = Pharaoh (as Kings); Beit-Shemesh = Beth-shemesh, 'the Beit-Shimshite' = the Beth-shemite; Ashqelon = Ashkelon; Qiryat-Ye'arim = Kiriath-jearim; Golyat = Goliath; Sha'ul = Saul; Yishai = Jesse; Eli'av = Eliab; Avinadav = Abinadab; Avner = Abner; Beit-Lechem = Bethlehem, 'the Beit-Lechemite' = the Bethlehemite, 'the Efratite' = the Ephrathite; Yehudah = Judah; Sokhoh = Socoh; Efes-Dammim = Ephes-dammim; Sha'arayim = Shaaraim; Eli, Dan, Shiloh, Ashdod, Dagon (central dagon entry), Shammah, Elah and Gai are identical in both forms. Pelishtim: the plural pəlištîm is 'the Pelishtim' as fixed by the central pelishtim-caphtor entry; the singular gentilic happəlištî is 'the Pelishtite' under the '-ite' rule (ASV 'the Philistines' / 'the Philistine').
entries.rationale: Former Prophets wave 1 (Josh 5, 6, 10; Judg 6, 13; 1 Sam 3, 5, 6, 17; Editor pass 2026-11-01, claude-opus-5-5). This entry is shared verbatim by the joshua-woh, judges-woh and 1-samuel-woh overlays; extend all three together. It applies, without change of substance, the Kings name convention that the founder ratified on 2026-11-01 (1-kings-woh / 2-kings-woh `hebrew-proper-name-transliteration-convention-kings`). The reasons given there hold for Joshua, Judges and Samuel, which continue the same narrative Hebrew: the corpus renders the Torah narratives and Kings with transliterated name forms (genesis-woh, exodus-woh, Kings), so the books between them should not switch to the KJV forms; transliteration keeps the theophoric and meaningful elements visible, which these chapters use (Yehoshua 'YHWH saves'; Shemu'el; the Ba'al element of Yerubba'al, which Judg 6:32 explains; Shimshon beside Beit-Shemesh, 'house of the sun'); and every name is given with its conventional English equivalent in this table and in the commentary at first occurrence in each chapter, so a reader can match the translation to the ASV and to the English editions of the Raëlian books, which quote these chapters as 'Joshua', 'Gideon', 'Samuel' and 'Goliath'. The convention is presentational and carries no interpretive content. Former Prophets specifics: (a) Azzah (Gaza) is transliterated, because it is not one of the few names that Kings keeps in English (Moab, Aram, Damascus, Horeb, Gilgal). (b) hanneḡeḇ is the region 'the Negev', where the ASV's 'the South' reads as a compass direction. (c) Gentilics follow the Kings '-ite' rule ('the Tishbite', 'the Shunammite', 'the Shomronites'): 'the Emorites', 'the Kena'anites', 'the Avi'ezrite', 'the Danites', 'the Ashdodites', 'the Eqronites', 'the Beit-Shimshite', 'the Pelishtite'. The corpus is not yet uniform on gentilics: genesis-woh writes 'the Emori', 'the Kena'ani' under central ten-nations-of-canaan (Gen 15:19-21), exodus-woh writes 'the Amorite', 'the Canaanite', and the plural 'Pelishtim' follows central pelishtim-caphtor (Gen 10:14), so the singular 'the Pelishtite' and the plural 'the Pelishtim' differ in form. A corpus-wide decision is a founder point in the wave-FP1 editor report; whichever form is chosen, the change is a mechanical substitution. (d) gibʿaṯ hāʿărālôṯ (Josh 5:3) is translated, as in the ASV, because it is a descriptive designation that the narrative explains, while Gilgal (5:9), whose explanation is a wordplay, stays a name. (e) Altar names are transliterated as names (YHWH-Shalom, Judg 6:24), with the meaning in commentary, as genesis-woh does for YHWH-yir'eh. Ratified at human sign-off (2026-11-01, zarazinsfuss), Former Prophets wave 1: the Former Prophets keep transliterated names with '-ite' gentilics, as Kings; the names stay split by book family for now (Torah English forms as published Exodus; Prophets and Writings English forms), with one corpus-wide naming decision later.

entries.wohChoice: The five clauses of the founder-ratified Kings entry `elohim-referent-and-article-conventions-kings`, unchanged, plus two clauses for constructions Kings did not meet. (1) YHWH referent with the Hebrew article (hāʾĕlōhîm): 'the Elohim' (Judg 6:20 'the messenger of the Elohim'; 6:36, 39; 13:6, 8, 9; 1 Sam 5:1, 2, 10, 11 'the ark of the Elohim', 5:11 'the hand of the Elohim'; 6:20 'YHWH, this holy Elohim', where the demonstrative stands for the article). (2) YHWH referent, anarthrous predicate, genitive or subject in direct speech: 'Elohim' without article (Judg 13:5, 7 'a Nazirite to Elohim'; 13:22 'we have seen Elohim', as genesis-woh Gen 32:31; 1 Sam 3:3 'the lamp of Elohim', 'the ark of Elohim'; 3:17 the Israelite oath 'So may Elohim do to you', as 1 Kgs 2:23; 17:46 'there is Elohim in Yisra'el', as 2 Kgs 1:3). (3) Construct with a possessor: 'YHWH your Elohim' (Josh 10:19; Judg 6:10, 26), 'the Elohim of Yisra'el' (Josh 10:40, 42; Judg 6:8; 1 Sam 5:7, 8, 10, 11; 6:3, 5), 'the Elohim of the armies of Yisra'el' (1 Sam 17:45). (4) Non-YHWH referent: lower-case 'elohim', number following the Hebrew ('the elohim of the Emorites', Judg 6:10; 'If he is an elohim', 6:31, of Ba'al; 'Dagon our elohim', 1 Sam 5:7; 'your elohim', 6:5; 'by his elohim', 17:43). (5) Generic class in a comparison or negation: lower-case 'elohim' (no site in this wave). (6) New: anarthrous ʾĕlōhîm as the subject of a narrative clause takes the article of the central elohim-as-translation narrative rule: 'And the Elohim did so' (Judg 6:40, wayyaʿaś ʾĕlōhîm kēn), the Hebrew difference from the articular vv 36, 39 being recorded in commentary. (7) New: anarthrous ʾĕlōhîm with an attributive adjective takes an English determiner, which English grammar requires: 'the armies of the living Elohim' (1 Sam 17:26, 36, maʿarḵôṯ ʾĕlōhîm ḥayyîm), with the anarthrous Hebrew and the plural adjective recorded in commentary.
entries.rationale: Former Prophets wave 1 (Josh 5, 6, 10; Judg 6, 13; 1 Sam 3, 5, 6, 17; Editor pass 2026-11-01, claude-opus-5-5). This entry is shared verbatim by the joshua-woh, judges-woh and 1-samuel-woh overlays; extend all three together. The Kings entry (ratified 2026-11-01) supplements the central elohim-as-translation convention, which keeps the plural 'Elohim' untranslated and sets the narrative article, with a referent rule: a capital for YHWH and lower case for any other god, so that contrasts the narrative depends on stay visible (Carmel, 1 Kgs 18; Ba'al-Zevuv, 2 Kgs 1). Judges and Samuel are built on the same contrast: Yo'ash's 'If he is an elohim, let him contend for himself' (Judg 6:31) answers the Ba'al cult as Eliyahu's 'for he is an elohim' does (1 Kgs 18:27), and 1 Sam 5 sets 'Dagon our elohim' (5:7) against the ark of 'the Elohim of Yisra'el'. The article follows the Hebrew in predicate, genitive and direct-speech positions, since adding 'the' there turns a classifying expression into an identification the Hebrew does not make (BDB ʾĕlōhîm 3). Two constructions occur here that Kings did not meet. (6) The Kings entry states that 'the narrative-subject article rule of the central entry is unaffected', and its anarthrous clause covers predicates, genitives and subjects in direct speech; an anarthrous narrative subject (Judg 6:40, after articular hāʾĕlōhîm in vv 36, 39) therefore falls under the central narrative rule and is rendered 'the Elohim'. The two Hebrew forms then look alike in English, and the commentary records the difference; dropping the article in narrative would reintroduce the singular proper-name reading the central entry was written to avoid. (7) maʿarḵôṯ ʾĕlōhîm ḥayyîm (1 Sam 17:26, 36; cf. Deut 5:23 [ET 5:26]; Jer 10:10; 23:36) is anarthrous, but an English attributive adjective needs a determiner ('the armies of living Elohim' is not idiomatic English), so the article is supplied as the ASV does ('the living God'); the commentary records that the Hebrew has no article and that the adjective ḥayyîm is plural in agreement with the form ʾĕlōhîm, unlike ʾēl ḥay (Josh 3:10; Hos 2:1 [ET 1:10]). The capital/lower-case distinction is an editorial device, since Hebrew script has no case.

entries.partOfSpeech: construct noun phrase used as a prophetic title
entries.literal: man of the God / a man of God
entries.standardEnglish: man of God (ASV, KJV, NRSV, NJPS)
entries.wohChoice: As the founder-ratified Kings entry `ish-ha-elohim-man-of-the-elohim-prophetic-title-kings`: 'man of the Elohim' where the Hebrew has the article, 'a man of Elohim' where it does not. Sites in this wave: 'The man of the Elohim came to me' (Judg 13:6; ASV 'A man of God') and 'let the man of the Elohim whom you sent come again' (13:8), both articular.
entries.rationale: Former Prophets wave 1 (Josh 5, 6, 10; Judg 6, 13; 1 Sam 3, 5, 6, 17; Editor pass 2026-11-01, claude-opus-5-5). This entry is shared verbatim by the joshua-woh, judges-woh and 1-samuel-woh overlays; extend all three together. ʾîš (hā)ʾĕlōhîm designates a person who belongs to and acts for the deity (BDB ʾîš 5); Kings uses it of Eliyahu, Elisha and the prophet of 1 Kgs 13, and the central elohim-as-translation convention excludes the rendering 'man of God'. The Kings entry renders the Hebrew article where it stands, because the alternation carries meaning in 2 Kgs 1:9-13, and records that the article on the genitive makes the whole chain definite (GKC §127a; Joüon-Muraoka §139a). In Judg 13:6 Manoach's wife uses the articular title at the first mention, before she knows what the figure is, and then compares his appearance with that of 'the messenger of the Elohim'. The definite English 'The man of the Elohim' follows the Hebrew; the ASV's indefinite 'A man of God' is a defensible English idiom for a first mention, and the commentary records it. The title used here of the figure later identified as the malʾaḵ YHWH (13:16, 21) is the same title Kings uses of human prophets, and the translation does not decide between the two by its rendering.

entries.lemma: nepeš 'throat, breath, life, living being, self'
entries.standardEnglish: soul (Josh 10:28-39, 'all the souls'; 1 Sam 17:55 'as thy soul liveth', ASV)
entries.wohChoice: As the founder-ratified Kings entry `nefesh-scope-and-spelling-kings`: 'nefesh' (transliterated) only where the nepeš is named as the life-component that departs or returns; idiomatic English elsewhere. Sites in this wave: 'every person that was in it' for kol-hannep̄eš ʾăšer-bāh (Josh 10:28, 30, 32, 35, 37 twice, 39; ASV 'all the souls'); 'As you yourself live' for the oath ḥê-nap̄šəḵā (1 Sam 17:55; ASV 'As thy soul liveth'), as 2 Kgs 2:2, 4, 6; 4:30.
entries.rationale: Former Prophets wave 1 (Josh 5, 6, 10; Judg 6, 13; 1 Sam 3, 5, 6, 17; Editor pass 2026-11-01, claude-opus-5-5). This entry is shared verbatim by the joshua-woh, judges-woh and 1-samuel-woh overlays; extend all three together. nepeš covers throat, breath, appetite, life, living being and the person him- or herself (HALOT nepeš 1-9; Wolff, Anthropology of the Old Testament, 1974), and the central glossary rejects the Platonic 'soul' for it (nefesh-chayah). The Kings entry transliterates it only where it names the life that leaves or returns to the body (1 Kgs 17:21-22, with central tzet-nephesh-departure-at-death-formula) and renders the idioms in English. In the conquest formula kol-hannep̄eš ʾăšer-bāh (Josh 10:28-39; 11:11) nepeš is the individual living being, the persons in a captured city (HALOT 'person'; NRSV 'every person in it'), so 'every person' renders it without the ASV's 'souls', which would suggest a technical sense the formula does not have. The oath ḥê-nap̄šəḵā swears by the addressee's life and is rendered 'as you yourself live' (cf. NJPS 'as you live'), the Kings rendering at 2 Kgs 2:2, 4, 6 and 4:30. The house spelling 'nefesh' (f for the spirantized p) is that of the Kings entry; no transliterated site occurs in this wave.

entries.literal: the wind/breath/spirit of YHWH; (a person's) spirit
entries.standardEnglish: the Spirit of Jehovah came upon (Judg 6:34), began to move (13:25) (ASV); there was no spirit in them any more (Josh 5:1, ASV)
entries.wohChoice: As the founder-ratified Kings entry `ruach-yhwh-and-prophetic-ruach-transliteration-kings`: 'the ruach of YHWH' for rûaḥ YHWH as an agent acting on a person (Kings: 1 Kgs 18:12; 22:24; 2 Kgs 2:16). Sites in this wave: 'But the ruach of YHWH clothed Gid'on' (Judg 6:34; the verb lāḇəšâ rendered literally, ASV 'came upon') and 'And the ruach of YHWH began to move him' (Judg 13:25; pāʿam 'move', ASV). The human rûaḥ in the sense of courage or vital energy is translated 'spirit' in lower case: 'there was no more spirit in them' (Josh 5:1; cf. 1 Kgs 10:5).
entries.rationale: Former Prophets wave 1 (Josh 5, 6, 10; Judg 6, 13; 1 Sam 3, 5, 6, 17; Editor pass 2026-11-01, claude-opus-5-5). This entry is shared verbatim by the joshua-woh, judges-woh and 1-samuel-woh overlays; extend all three together. rûaḥ covers 'wind', 'breath' and 'spirit' (BDB; HALOT rûaḥ 1-11). The ASV capital 'Spirit of Jehovah' settles the reading in favour of the later doctrinal concept of a personal Holy Spirit, which the Hebrew does not specify; the Kings entry, ratified at human sign-off on 2026-11-01, therefore transliterates rûaḥ YHWH as 'the ruach of YHWH' wherever it is an agent acting on a person, as ezekiel-woh does at Ezek 37:1, and it is applied here so that the same expression reads alike across the Former Prophets. In Judges the rûaḥ YHWH is the power that comes on a deliverer and moves him to act (Block, Judges, Ruth, NAC 6, 1999; Webb, The Book of Judges, NICOT, 2012), and the book uses distinct verbs for its coming: hāyâ ʿal 'came upon' (3:10; 11:29), ṣālaḥ ʿal 'rushed upon' (14:6, 19; 15:14), lāḇaš 'clothed' (6:34) and pāʿam 'move, impel' (13:25). The translation keeps the noun constant and the verbs distinct. lāḇəšâ ʾeṯ-giḏʿôn is rendered literally 'clothed Gid'on', as the KJV margin and many commentators do (the rûaḥ takes the person as its garment; cf. 1 Chr 12:19; 2 Chr 24:20), instead of the ASV's levelling 'came upon'; pāʿam (13:25), whose noun means 'a beat, a step', keeps the ASV 'move'. The anthropological rûaḥ of Josh 5:1, the courage that fails the kings of Kena'an, is an ordinary English sense of 'spirit' and is translated. The entry is inferred, as its Kings source is: transliteration leaves a recognized ambiguity open, and the commentary sets out the readings without choosing.

entries.lemma: Ketiv ('what is written', the consonantal text) and Qere ('what is read', the Masoretic reading tradition)
entries.literal: the written consonants vs the vocalized reading
entries.standardEnglish: ASV and all major English versions translate the Qere, with occasional exceptions
entries.wohChoice: As the founder-ratified Kings entry `ketiv-qere-qere-translated-kings`: translate the Qere; record the Ketiv in commentary at every site. Sites in this wave (15 readings in 15 verses, as marked in the source edition): Josh 5:1 (K ʿbrnw 'we crossed' / Q ʿoḇrām 'they crossed'), 6:5 (K bə- / Q kə- 'when you hear'), 6:7 (K 'and they said' / Q 'and he said'), 6:9 (K perfect tqʿw / Q participle tōqəʿê 'who blew'), 6:13 (K participle / Q infinitive absolute hālôḵ); Judg 6:5 (K ybʾw, imperfect yāḇōʾû / Q ûḇāʾû), 13:17 (K 'your words' / Q 'your word'); 1 Sam 3:2 (K 'his eye' / Q 'his eyes'), 5:6, 5:9, 5:12, 6:4, 6:5 (K ʿŏp̄ālîm 'swellings' / Q ṭəḥōrîm 'tumors', governed also by `ofalim-tehorim-tumors-1-samuel-5-6`), 17:7 (K wḥṣ / Q wəʿēṣ 'shaft'), 17:23 (K 'from the caves' / Q 'from the ranks').
entries.rationale: Former Prophets wave 1 (Josh 5, 6, 10; Judg 6, 13; 1 Sam 3, 5, 6, 17; Editor pass 2026-11-01, claude-opus-5-5). This entry is shared verbatim by the joshua-woh, judges-woh and 1-samuel-woh overlays; extend all three together. The Leningrad Codex marks each Ketiv/Qere pair, and the Masoretic tradition reads the Qere; English translation, including the ASV baseline, follows the Qere in all but a handful of cases (Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, 3rd ed., 2012). The Kings entry, ratified 2026-11-01, translates the Qere and records the Ketiv, so that the English follows the reading tradition and the consonantal text stays auditable. Of the fifteen readings here, three depart from the ASV, which follows the Ketiv at Josh 5:1 ('until we were passed over'), 6:7 ('And they said') and Judg 13:17 ('thy words'); the Qere is translated there as everywhere and the ASV reading is recorded in commentary. The five ʿŏp̄ālîm / ṭəḥōrîm sites of 1 Sam 5-6 are a single lexical substitution listed in b. Megillah 25b among readings substituted for delicacy; the rendering 'tumors' is governed by the 1-samuel-woh entry `ofalim-tehorim-tumors-1-samuel-5-6`. The anomalous final aleph of hehāləḵûʾ (Josh 10:24) is not a Ketiv/Qere in the source edition and is recorded under the MT-baseline entry.

entries.standardEnglish: ASV follows the MT at most of these sites; NRSV and other modern versions adopt the versional reading at several (Josh 6:18; 1 Sam 17:4 note; 17:32)
entries.wohChoice: As the founder-ratified Kings entry `mt-baseline-at-versional-cruxes-and-versification-kings`: translate the MT vocalization, wording and verse division; give the versional reading in commentary; supply no subject or word the Hebrew leaves unexpressed. Sites in this wave. Joshua: 5:14 'No' (MT lōʾ; some MSS, LXX, Syriac lô 'to him'); 6:9, 13 the subject of 'blowing' left unexpressed (ASV supplies '[the priests]'); 6:18 'lest when you have devoted it' (MT taḥărîmû; LXX 'lest you covet', = taḥmədû); 6:20 MT order of shout and blast, 'they blew' impersonal; 6:26 (LXX adds the fulfilment by Hiel, cf. 1 Kgs 16:34; not translated); 10:10 YHWH as subject of the following verbs; 10:13 the citation of the Book of Yashar (absent from the LXX); 10:15 and 10:43 (absent from the LXX; translated); 10:24 hehāləḵûʾ with anomalous final aleph, translated as the ordinary verb. Judges: 6:7-10 (absent from 4QJudgᵃ; translated); 6:13, 15 the vocalizations ʾăḏōnî 'my lord' and ʾăḏōnāy 'Lord'; 6:14 'YHWH turned to him' (LXX 'the messenger of YHWH'); 13:19 'and he did wondrously', subject unexpressed (ASV '[the angel]'; LXX 'to the Lord who works wonders'). 1 Samuel: 3:13 məqalləlîm lāhem 'bringing a curse on themselves' (a tiqqun soferim; LXX 'speaking evil of God'); 3:21 (LXX longer; not translated); 5:4 'only Dagon was left to him', no supplement (ASV '[the stump of]'); 5:6 (LXX plus on the mice; not translated); 6:19 'looked into the ark' and 'seventy men, fifty thousand men' (LXX 'the sons of Jeconiah'; Josephus and some MSS 'seventy'); 17:4 'six cubits and a span' (LXX, 4QSamᵃ, Josephus 'four'); 17:12 'advanced among men' (Lucianic Greek, Syriac 'in years'); the full MT of 1 Sam 17, including the pluses absent from LXX Vaticanus (vv 12-31, 41, 48b, 50, 55-58), translated without marking; 17:32 'no man's heart' (LXX 'my lord's'); 17:52 'Gai' (LXX 'Gath'). The single departure from the MT in this wave, ratified at human sign-off (2026-11-01) as a narrow exception, 1 Sam 6:18 'the great stone' for MT ʾāḇēl, is governed by the 1-samuel-woh entry `even-ha-gedolah-the-great-stone-1-samuel-6-18`.
entries.rationale: Former Prophets wave 1 (Josh 5, 6, 10; Judg 6, 13; 1 Sam 3, 5, 6, 17; Editor pass 2026-11-01, claude-opus-5-5). This entry is shared verbatim by the joshua-woh, judges-woh and 1-samuel-woh overlays; extend all three together. The Wheel of Heaven Translation translates the Masoretic Text and records ancient-version and conjectural readings in the apparatus (genesis-woh, exodus-woh; the Kings entry, ratified 2026-11-01). At each site listed the MT gives a construable sense, even where most modern commentators prefer another reading: lōʾ in Josh 5:14 can answer 'neither' to Yehoshua's either-or question (Nelson, Joshua, OTL, 1997); taḥărîmû in 6:18 makes sense as 'having devoted (the city), do not then take from it'; the narrator's alternation of the messenger and YHWH in Judg 6:11-24 is characteristic of the malʾaḵ YHWH narratives and is not an error to be harmonized; the tiqqun soferim of 1 Sam 3:13 reads intelligibly as it stands; and the larger figure for Golyat, the asyndetic 'seventy men, fifty thousand men' and the long form of 1 Sam 17 are readings of the transmitted Hebrew whose relation to the shorter or smaller Greek and Qumran readings is a matter of textual history (Barthélemy, Gooding, Lust and Tov, The Story of David and Goliath, OBO 73, 1986; McCarter, I Samuel, AB 8, 1980), which the commentary sets out without adopting. Supplying a subject the Hebrew leaves unexpressed (Josh 6:9, 13, 20; Judg 13:19) would be an interpretive addition, so the line keeps the Hebrew's indeterminacy. Verse numbers follow the Hebrew; in these chapters the English and Hebrew verse divisions agree.

entries.wohChoice: 'YHWH of hosts', as the founder-ratified Kings entry `yhwh-tsevaot-yhwh-of-hosts-kings` and isaiah-woh. Site in this wave: 'in the name of YHWH of hosts, the Elohim of the armies of Yisra'el' (1 Sam 17:45).
entries.rationale: Former Prophets wave 1 (Josh 5, 6, 10; Judg 6, 13; 1 Sam 3, 5, 6, 17; Editor pass 2026-11-01, claude-opus-5-5). This entry is shared verbatim by the joshua-woh, judges-woh and 1-samuel-woh overlays; extend all three together. The title is rendered as in Kings and Isaiah, keeping the corpus divine-name style 'YHWH' and the ASV noun 'hosts'. Its grammar (a proper name in apparent construct) and the referent of the 'hosts' (Israel's armies, the heavenly host, the divine assembly) are debated (Mettinger, The Dethronement of Sabaoth, 1982; Cross, Canaanite Myth and Hebrew Epic, 1973), and 'hosts' leaves both open. At 1 Sam 17:45 the title is followed by the apposition 'the Elohim of the armies (maʿarḵôṯ) of Yisra'el', which connects the 'hosts' with Israel's battle lines in David's mouth; the apposition is rendered under the elohim-referent entry (clause 3), and 'armies' keeps the ASV rendering of maʿarḵôṯ used throughout the chapter. The title first occurs in the Hebrew Bible at 1 Sam 1:3, in connection with the Shiloh sanctuary of the ark. Josh 5:14 śar-ṣəḇāʾ-YHWH 'captain of the host of YHWH' uses the singular ṣāḇāʾ and is governed by the joshua-woh entry `sar-tzeva-yhwh-captain-of-the-host-of-yhwh-joshua-5`.

entries.lemma: baʿal 'owner, lord, husband'; as a divine name, the West-Semitic storm god Baal
entries.partOfSpeech: divine name (normally with the article in Hebrew prose)
entries.wohChoice: 'Ba'al' without the English article, as the founder-ratified Kings entry `habbaal-baal-hebrew-bible-rendering-kings`. Sites in this wave: 'the altar of Ba'al' (Judg 6:25, 28, 30); 'Will you contend for Ba'al?' (6:31); 'Let Ba'al contend against him' and the name Yerubba'al (6:32).
entries.rationale: Former Prophets wave 1 (Josh 5, 6, 10; Judg 6, 13; 1 Sam 3, 5, 6, 17; Editor pass 2026-11-01, claude-opus-5-5). This entry is shared verbatim by the joshua-woh, judges-woh and 1-samuel-woh overlays; extend all three together. Hebrew prose writes the god's name with the article (habbaʿal), a remnant of its origin as the title 'the Lord'; English treats it as a proper name, and the ASV, NRSV and NJPS omit the article, as Kings does. The spelling with the apostrophe for ʿayin follows the Kings and genesis-woh transliteration practice and governs the theophoric name Yerubba'al, whose explanation in Judg 6:32 (yāreḇ bô habbaʿal 'let Ba'al contend against him') plays on the god's name; the name probably meant 'Ba'al contends' or 'Ba'al is great', and later scribes deformed it to Yerubbeshet (2 Sam 11:21) (Block, Judges, Ruth, NAC 6, 1999). The Ugaritic deity is governed by central baal-ugaritic-baalu-storm-god-cross-corpus-hebrew-bible-polemic, of which this entry is the Hebrew-Bible counterpart.

entries.lemma: śar 'official, commander, prince' in construct with ṣāḇāʾ 'army, host'
entries.literal: commander of the army of YHWH
entries.standardEnglish: prince of the host of Jehovah (ASV); captain of the host of the LORD (KJV); commander of the army of the LORD (NRSV, NJPS)
entries.wohChoice: 'the captain of the host of YHWH' (Josh 5:14, 15)
entries.rationale: śar haṣṣāḇāʾ is the ordinary Hebrew title of an army commander, and the corpus renders it 'captain of the host' as the ASV does elsewhere (1 Kgs 1:19, 25; 2:32; 1 Sam 17:55, Avner); the central tzeva-ha-shamayim-host-of-the-heavens-divine-council-cross-corpus entry keeps 'host' for ṣāḇāʾ so that the lexical link between Israel's army and the heavenly host stays visible. The ASV's 'prince' here (KJV 'captain') singles this one occurrence out with a courtly word, which the Hebrew does not do, so the corpus rendering is used; 'commander of the army' (NRSV, NJPS) would be accurate but would break the 'host' link. The construct with YHWH leaves open whether the 'host' is the heavenly army (1 Kgs 22:19) or Israel's army as YHWH's (Ex 12:41 'all the hosts of YHWH went out'), and whether the figure is the malʾaḵ YHWH, as many interpreters hold (cf. Num 22:23, 31, the messenger with the drawn sword), an angelic commander (cf. Dan 10:13, 21 śar), or a manifestation of YHWH, since the command of 5:15 repeats Ex 3:5 (Boling and Wright, Joshua, AB 6, 1982; Nelson, Joshua, OTL, 1997; Butler, Joshua, WBC 7, 1983); the Hebrew of 5:13-15 does not use malʾāḵ, and the central malakh-yhwh-messenger entry is not cited there. The English canon quotation (The Book Which Tells the Truth, ch. 3) reads 'the captain of the host of Yahweh', which coincides with the rendering; its reading of the figure is confined to a labelled reception note. The entry is direct: the rendering is the established English equivalent of the title and adds no interpretation.

entries.lemma: ḥērem 'what is devoted (to the deity), the ban'; ḥrm Hiphil 'devote (to destruction), put under the ban'
entries.literal: a thing set apart for the deity (by destruction); to devote / consign to the ban
entries.standardEnglish: devoted / the devoted thing / accursed (noun, ASV Josh 6:17-18); utterly destroyed (verb, ASV); devoted to destruction (NRSV Josh 6:21)
entries.wohChoice: noun 'devoted' / 'the devoted thing' throughout ('the city shall be devoted', Josh 6:17; 'keep yourselves from the devoted thing ... and so make the camp of Yisra'el a devoted thing', 6:18, ASV 'accursed'); Hiphil verb 'devote to destruction' throughout ('they devoted to destruction', 6:21; 10:1, 28, 35, 37, 39, 40; ASV 'utterly destroyed')
entries.rationale: ḥērem designates what is withdrawn from human use and handed over to the deity, in war normally by destruction (Lev 27:28-29; Num 21:2-3; Deut 7:2, 26; 20:16-18); the Moabite stone uses the same verb of Mesha's war against Israel (line 17, 'I devoted it to Ashtar-Kemosh'), so the institution is a shared West-Semitic war practice, not an Israelite peculiarity (Stern, The Biblical Ḥerem, BJS 211, 1991; Lohfink, TDOT V, ḥāram; Nelson, Joshua, OTL, 1997). The ASV distributes the root over 'devoted', 'devoted thing', 'accursed' and 'utterly destroyed', so that a reader cannot see that Josh 6:21 and the city-by-city refrain of Josh 10 carry out the ḥērem announced at 6:17, or that 6:18 plays on the noun and the verb three times. The translation renders the noun 'devoted' / 'the devoted thing' and the verb 'devote to destruction' at every site, as the NRSV does at 6:21: the verbal rendering names both the sacral transfer and the destruction that the Hiphil denotes in war (HALOT ḥrm I hif.). At 6:18 wəśamtem ʾeṯ-maḥănēh yiśrāʾēl ləḥērem is rendered 'and so make the camp of Yisra'el a devoted thing', since taking from the ḥērem transfers its status to the camp, which ch. 7 narrates. The entry is lexical and direct; it neither softens nor sharpens the moral weight of the conquest narratives, which the commentary leaves to the literature. Central-promotion candidate: ḥērem recurs in Numbers, Deuteronomy, Judges and 1 Samuel (15:3-21); if a parallel Editor creates a central entry for the Torah occurrences, this overlay entry should merge into it with these sites in its appliesTo. Ratified at human sign-off (2026-11-01, zarazinsfuss), Former Prophets wave 1: ḥērem = 'devote(d) to destruction' (Num 21:2-3 aligned in the Torah wave), to be promoted to a central entry.

entries.source: וְהֵרִיעוּ ... תְּרוּעָה גְדוֹלָה ; וְנָפְלָה חוֹמַת הָעִיר תַּחְתֶּיהָ ; תָּקַע
entries.translit: wəhērîʿû ... tərûʿâ ḡəḏôlâ ; wənāp̄əlâ ḥômaṯ hāʿîr taḥteyhā ; tāqaʿ
entries.lemma: rûaʿ Hiphil 'raise a shout / sound an alarm'; tərûʿâ 'shout, war cry, horn signal'; tāqaʿ 'blow (a horn)'
entries.partOfSpeech: verbs and noun of the Jericho rite
entries.literal: they shall raise a great shout; the wall of the city shall fall beneath itself; blow
entries.standardEnglish: shout with a great shout; the wall of the city shall fall down flat; blow (ASV)
entries.wohChoice: 'shout' / 'shout with a great shout' for rûaʿ / tərûʿâ (Josh 6:5, 10, 16, 20); 'blow' for tāqaʿ (6:4, 8, 9, 13, 16, 20); 'make a long blast' for māšaḵ bəqeren (6:5); 'fall down flat' for nāp̄əlâ ... taḥteyhā (6:5, 20) (ASV throughout)
entries.rationale: The Jericho rite distinguishes two sound actions: the priests blow (tāqaʿ) the shofars and draw out (māšaḵ) a long note, and the people shout (rûaʿ Hiphil) a tərûʿâ. tərûʿâ is both the war cry of an army (1 Sam 17:20, 52; Amos 1:14) and the name of a horn signal (Num 10:5-9; 31:6), and in Josh 6 the subject of the verb is 'the people' and its sound is 'your voice' (6:10), so the ASV 'shout with a great shout' is accurate and is kept; reading it as a horn blast would contradict 6:10 and 6:20. nāp̄əlâ ... taḥteyhā is literally 'shall fall beneath itself / in its place', i.e. collapse where it stands (BDB taḥaṯ 2a), and the ASV's 'fall down flat' renders the idiom without technical overtones. The English canon quotation of 6:5 (The Book Which Tells the Truth, ch. 3, from the French Bible) has 'the trumpet' and reads the instrument as an ultrasonic device; the line keeps the Hebrew's ram's horn (central shofar entry) and the plain verbs, and that reading is confined to a labelled reception note. Archaeological discussion of Jericho's walls (Kenyon's excavations, the absence of a Late Bronze city wall) is outside the translation and is not argued in the apparatus. The entry is direct: it keeps the established English renderings and records the lexical basis.

entries.literal: great stones from the skies ... the stones of the hail
entries.standardEnglish: great stones from heaven ... the hailstones (ASV)
entries.wohChoice: 'great stones from the skies ... the hailstones' (Josh 10:11)
entries.rationale: The verse names the missiles twice: first as ʾăḇānîm gəḏōlôṯ 'great stones' thrown down by YHWH from šāmayim, then, in the same sentence, as ʾaḇnê habbārāḏ 'the stones of the hail', an ordinary Hebrew expression for hailstones (Isa 30:30 ʾeḇen bārāḏ; cf. Ezek 13:11, 13; 38:22 ʾaḇnê ʾelgāḇîš; Ex 9:18-26). The narrator therefore identifies the 'great stones' as hail, and both expressions are rendered literally, so the reader sees the identification the Hebrew makes. šāmayim is 'the skies' under the register rule of the central shamayim entry (weather and the physical sky; ASV and the English canon quotation 'from heaven'), as with fire 'from the skies' at 2 Kgs 1:10-14. Hail as YHWH's weapon belongs to the divine-warrior imagery of the Hebrew Bible (Ex 9:23-25; Job 38:22-23, central otzrot-sheleg-barad; Ps 18:13-14; Isa 30:30; Ezek 38:22) (Nelson, Joshua, OTL, 1997; Butler, Joshua, WBC 7, 1983). The Book Which Tells the Truth (ch. 3) quotes the verse and reads it as an aerial bombardment; that reading is confined to a labelled reception note, and the line uses no technical vocabulary. The entry is direct: it renders the Hebrew nouns as they stand.

entries.source: שֶׁמֶשׁ בְּגִבְעוֹן דּוֹם וְיָרֵחַ בְּעֵמֶק אַיָּלוֹן ; וַיִּדֹּם הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ וְיָרֵחַ עָמָד ; וַיַּעֲמֹד הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ
entries.translit: šemeš bəḡiḇʿôn dôm wəyārēaḥ bəʿēmeq ʾayyālôn ; wayyiddōm haššemeš wəyārēaḥ ʿāmāḏ ; wayyaʿămōḏ haššemeš
entries.lemma: dāmam 'be still, be silent, wait'; ʿāmaḏ 'stand, stop'
entries.literal: Sun, be still at Gibeon ... and the sun was still, and the moon stood ... and the sun stood
entries.standardEnglish: Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon; And thou, Moon, in the valley of Aijalon. And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed ... And the sun stayed in the midst of heaven (ASV)
entries.wohChoice: 'Sun, stand still at Giv'on, and moon, in the valley of Ayyalon' (Josh 10:12); 'And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed ... And the sun stayed in the midst of the skies and did not hasten to go down for about a whole day' (10:13)
entries.rationale: dôm is the imperative of dāmam, whose range is 'be still, be motionless, be silent, wait' (BDB; HALOT); the parallel verb ʿāmaḏ 'stand, stop' in v 13 fixes the sense 'stand still' in the narrative's own understanding, and the ASV renderings are kept. Interpreters divide on what the couplet (12b-13a, cited from the Book of Yashar) originally asked: a halt of the sun's course (the traditional reading, which v 13b and v 14 adopt); a cessation of the sun's light or heat, by eclipse or cloud (dāmam as 'be silent / cease'); or, comparing Mesopotamian omen texts in which the sun and moon 'stand' in a favourable opposition on a given day, a prayer for a good omen (Holladay, 'The Day(s) the Moon Stood Still', JBL 87, 1968; Walton, 'Joshua 10:12-15 and Mesopotamian Celestial Omen Texts', in Millard, Hoffmeier and Baker (eds.), Faith, Tradition, and History, 1994). The translation renders the verbs in their primary sense and records the alternatives in commentary without choosing; it does not render dôm 'be silent' or 'wait', which would commit the line to one of the reinterpretations. šāmayim in v 13 is the physical sky ('in the midst of the skies', central shamayim). The Book Which Tells the Truth (ch. 3) reads 'about a whole day' as the duration of a lightning war that people took for a halt of the sun; that reading is confined to a labelled reception note. The couplet is printed as prose, as the chapter-file format has one English line per verse; its poetic form is described in commentary.

entries.partOfSpeech: construct noun phrase, title of a lost book
entries.standardEnglish: the book of Jashar (ASV); the Book of the Upright (some modern versions)
entries.wohChoice: 'the Book of Yashar' (Josh 10:13; the same rendering is recommended for 2 Sam 1:18)
entries.rationale: The Book of Yashar is a lost collection of poetry cited as a source at Josh 10:13 (the sun-and-moon couplet) and 2 Sam 1:18 (David's lament for Sha'ul and Yonatan); the LXX of 1 Kgs 8:53a cites a 'book of the song' (biblion tēs ōdēs, = sēp̄er haššîr), which many take for the same title with metathesis of yšr / šyr (Nelson, Joshua, OTL, 1997; Cogan, 1 Kings, AB 10, 2001). The title is treated as a proper name and transliterated, as the ASV does ('Jashar'), with the tz/y conventions of the name entry; translating it ('the Book of the Upright') would make a title of uncertain meaning look transparent. The LXX of Josh 10 lacks the reference, which the MT-baseline entry records. Later works called 'the Book of Jasher' (a medieval Hebrew midrash, 1625; an 18th-century English forgery) have no connection with the lost book, and the commentary says so. The entry is direct: the rendering is the established English title in transliteration.
